Lesson plan: How Chatbots Write

Tokens, probabilities and attention: what really happens when a chatbot writes an answer.

By the end of the lesson, students can

  • explain how text becomes tokens, and tokens become numbers;
  • describe next-token prediction, and how temperature changes the choice of the next word;
  • explain what attention does, and why a chatbot can sound sure and still be wrong.

Warm-up

Your phone's keyboard suggests the next word. How do you think it knows what to suggest?

Students may say that it remembers what they type. Lead to the idea of probabilities: the keyboard guesses the likeliest next word. Chatbots do the same, with a much bigger model.

Reading

Students read the lesson “How Chatbots Write”. Students look for how “unbelievable” is cut into tokens, what “it” means in the robot sentence, and what the T in GPT stands for.

Activity: Mini-lab “Temperature dial”

  1. Students open the mini-lab in lesson 9 and read the start of the sentence and the six possible next words.
  2. At temperature 1.0 they press “Generate 10” and note which words were picked.
  3. They turn the dial to 0.2 and to 2.0, write the probabilities into the worksheet's table, and press “Generate 10” each time.
  4. They open “Show the maths” and follow one row of the table: the score, the score ÷ T, then the probability.

For students who finish early

Fast finishers predict, before trying, what the probabilities will look like at temperature 0.5, then check.

Discussion questions

  • Why does a chatbot sometimes give a different answer to the same question?
  • Would you want a low or a high temperature for a chatbot that helps with homework? For one that writes song lyrics?
  • A chatbot picks likely words, not checked facts. What does that mean for how you use it?
  • Russian often needs more tokens than English for the same text. Why might that matter?

Exit ticket

Explain in your own words what “next-token prediction” means.

Quick check. “The robot dropped the box because it was heavy.” What lets a language model work out that “it” means the box?
Right answer: Attention: weighing how much each earlier word matters

Easier and harder

Easier. Write the robot sentence on the board, and let students draw an arrow from “it” to the word it means, first with “heavy”, then with “clumsy”.

Harder. Students work out the softmax by hand for three scores of their own at temperature 1 (with e ≈ 2.718 and a calculator) and check that the probabilities add up to 100%.
